info.bio:
The Marvelettes, grupo de soul formado en 1960 por Katherine Anderson, Anne Bogan, Juanita Cowart, Gladys Horton, Georgeanna Tillman y Wanda Young en Michigan.

Probablemente son el grupo de Motown más orientado hacie el pop, y a pesar de que nunca consiguieron el éxito de The Supremes, Mary Wells o Martha Reeves, tuvieron éxitos como el número uno "Please Mr Postman" en 1961. Otros de sus hits fueron "Playboy", "Twistin' Postman" y "Beechwood 4-5789".

scenes.name: Motown: Supremes y Holland-Dozier-Holland
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los grupos de Tamla/Motown ocuparon el hueco de los girl groups: Martha and the Vandellas («Heat Wave», «Dancing in the Street», «Nowhere to Run»), Gladys Knight, las Marvelettes, las Velvelettes y, sobre todo, las Supremes, el grupo pop americano de más éxito del momento (seis números 1 en dos años). Tres amigas del proyecto Brewster-Douglass, las «Supremes sin éxitos» hasta «Where Did Our Love Go» (1964): Berry Gordy vio en ellas el caballo de Troya para entrar en el mercado blanco, con los Funk Brothers, la escritura «psicológica» de Holland-Dozier-Holland (playlets femeninos sobre el amor como adicción, música dura contra letras sumisas) y el departamento de Artist Development de Maxine Powell y Cholly Atkins. Su imagen de espectáculo (Copacabana, pelucas) contrastaba con la nueva bohemia rock, como en su incómodo encuentro con unos Beatles fumados. Diana Ross ardía: seis números 1 y aún las trataban como a un grupo cualquiera.

scenes.name: El soul conquista Gran Bretaña
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 26 de octubre «Reach Out I’ll Be There» de los Four Tops, con la flauta de aire oriental, el fraseo dylaniano de Lamont Dozier y la interpretación de su vida de Levi Stubbs, desbancó a «Distant Drums» y fue número 1: el momento en que la música negra americana ocupó el centro de la cultura juvenil británica, al revés que en el boom del beat. Lo habían preparado durante años los entusiastas: Dave Godin, que fundó en 1963 la Tamla Motown Appreciation Society, viajó a Detroit, llevó «Where Did Our Love Go» a los piratas y bautizó el sello Tamla Motown (marzo de 1965, con una gira de la revista que fracasó fuera de Londres); Guy Stevens, que pinchaba discos negros en el Scene y dirigió Sue Records para Chris Blackwell; Roger Eagle en el Twisted Wheel de Mánchester; Tony Hall promocionando Atlantic («In the Midnight Hour», el «My Girl» de Otis Redding); el DJ Jeff Dexter mezclando soul y ska en Tiles, el club subterráneo de Oxford Street del mod de masas que visitó Tom Wolfe. En otoño de 1966 Atlantic y Motown copaban las listas; Otis Redding metió a 8.000 personas en Tiles; los Four Tops arrasaron en el Savile de Brian Epstein el 13 de noviembre. El racismo, aun así, seguía ahí.

scenes.name: Electro de Los Ángeles: Wreckin’ Cru y Uncle Jamm’s Army
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Las cintas del hip hop llegaban a la Costa Oeste con los familiares y los soldados; allí, entre la herencia de los disturbios de Watts (1965) y el «blockbusting» que convirtió Compton en una ciudad negra, la escena de DJs móviles se volcó en Bambaataa y la electrónica. Alonzo Williams, antes Disco Lonzo, dirigió el Eve After Dark desde 1979 con concursos de baile y rap (Ice-T ganó uno con Kurtis Blow de jurado) y formó la World Class Wreckin’ Cru, grupo de electro-rap con trajes de lentejuelas: DJ Yella, Cli-N-Tel y Dr. Dre, vecino suyo que mezclaba «Please Mr. Postman» con un break. Davy DMX, el DJ de Kurtis Blow, enseñó a Yella, Yella a Dre y Dre a los demás; «Slice» y «Surgery» salieron en Kru-Cut y Macola antes de fichar por CBS/Epic. Su rival, el Uncle Jamm’s Army de Rodger Clayton y Gid Martin, juntaba a diez mil chavales en el Sports Arena solo con DJs y crió a Ice-T, DJ Pooh y Egyptian Lover; se arrancaban los carteles a cinco dólares la pieza. En el club Radio (luego Radiotron), más club punk que otra cosa, Chris «The Glove» Taylor, que scratcheaba «como un batería», puso la música de Breakin’ (1984) y produjo con Ice-T «Reckless».

podcast.title: Auditioning for Motown
podcast.body: After placing fourth in a talent contest offering a Motown audition as a prize, The Cassin Yet impressed the label but were told they needed to present original material to be signed. This led to the creation of "Please Mr. Postman," which later secured their contract. "The group came forth, but one of their teachers, Shirley Sharply, knew the person from Motown who was arranging the auditions, and persuaded them to offer auditions to the top five, rather than just to the winners."

podcast.title: Dual Lead Vocal Attempt as The Darnells
podcast.body: Motown experimented with changing the group's dynamic by releasing a single under the name "The Darnells," featuring Gladys Horton and Wonder Young on dual lead vocals, backed by Motown's in-house group, The Andantes. This endeavor, however, proved unsuccessful. "The record was put out under the name The Darnells, but was unsuccessful."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Success Over The Supremes
podcast.body: The Marvelettes were signed by Motown Records and achieved significant success as "major stars," effectively "leapfrogging" over The Supremes in terms of chart performance and commercial impact during their early careers. "Motown had signed the Maratholettes, and they'd leapfogged over the Supremes to become major stars."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Erosion of Group Cohesion
podcast.body: The departure of Juanita and Georgiana significantly impacted the group's internal dynamics, as they had been the "glue" that held the initial members together. Catherine Anderson later noted that the remaining members, who hadn't known each other prior, transitioned from being friends to merely "acquaintances and co-workers." "Juanita and Georgiana had been the glue holding the group together. They'd been the ones who had been friends with all the others."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Followers of The Shirelles' Template
podcast.body: The Marvelettes are listed as one of the prominent girl groups that followed in the footsteps of The Shirelles, who set the template for the booming girl group sound of the 1960s. "The Supremes, the Marvelettes, the crystals, the Ronettes, and the rest, all were following in the Chirrells footsteps."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: Formation as The Cassin Yet
podcast.body: Gladys Horton formed a new group for a high school talent contest, initially jokingly naming themselves The Cassin Yet. The name, a self-deprecating reference to their perceived vocal abilities ("because they can't sing yet"), was used for their performance, which placed fourth but secured them a Motown audition. "The group she formed originally jokingly named themselves The Cassin Yet, because they can't sing yet, and that was the name under which they performed at the talent contest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Georgia Dobbins' Father's Refusal to Sign Contract
podcast.body: Georgia Dobbins, a key contributor to "Please Mr. Postman," was forced to quit the group when her father refused to counter-sign her record contract because she was under 21 and he believed the entertainment industry was "sinful." Her mother was too ill to sign, and this led to Georgia giving up singing entirely until 1978. "Her father hadn't known she was singing, until she brought the record contract home for him to counter sign."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Georgiana Tillman's Illness and Early Death
podcast.body: Georgiana Tillman, who had been diagnosed with sickle cell anemia as a child, became increasingly ill from the strain of constant touring. She was later diagnosed with lupus, an autoimmune disease that was often a death sentence at the time, leading her to retire from music and work as a secretary for Motown. She died in 1980 at the age of 36. "Eventually it was realised that she had lupus, an autoimmune disease which is now largely treatable if not curable, but at the time was often a death sentence."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Gladys Horton's Departure and Group Priority
podcast.body: Gladys Horton's decision to leave the group in 1967 lowered The Marvelettes' priority within Motown. Although Wonder Young was the lead singer by then, the group was still informally considered "Gladys' group" by Motown staff due to her initial leadership role. "This made the group an even lower priority for Motown. While Wander was by now the undisputed lead singer, within Motown there were thought of as Gladys' group, as she'd been the leader in the beginning."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Impact of Touring on Recording Practices
podcast.body: By the mid-1960s, while records were still released as by The Marvelettes, Smokey Robinson often only utilized Wonder Young for lead vocals, with The Andantes providing backing. This practice was justified by the group's constant touring schedule, making it easier to record without the full lineup. "By this point, while the records were getting released as by The Marvellettes, Robinson was only using Wander for lead vocals, and having the Andante's single or backing vocals."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Juanita's Departure Due to American Bandstand Mockery
podcast.body: Juanita (Winnie Cowatt) left the group after a humiliating experience on "American Bandstand." She mistakenly said Detroit was a suburb of Inkster instead of the other way around, leading to mockery that caused her to have a breakdown. "She felt so bad about this slip-up and the way she was mocked for it, so she had a breakdown and ended up leaving the group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Lack of Recognition at Motown Anniversaries
podcast.body: Despite being the first group to achieve a number one hit for Motown, none of the original Marvelettes members were invited to participate in any of the label's 25th, 40th, 50th, or 60th-anniversary celebrations or associated TV specials, which honored the label's history. "None of the members of the first group to hit number one on the label were invited to be part of any of them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Motor City Records Reunion Album
podcast.body: In the late 1980s, British DJ Ian Levine, who owned Motor City Records, persuaded Gladys Horton and Wonder Young to come out of retirement to record a new Marvelettes album. This reunion effort featured two new backing vocalists, Echo Johnson and Jean McLean, and included remakes of old hits and new songs. "He managed to persuade Gladys and Wanda out of retirement to make a new Marvillette's album with two new backing vocalists, Echo Johnson and Jean McLean."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Motown's Policy on Group Members and Touring
podcast.body: After "Please Mr. Postman" became a hit, Motown initially suggested sending "any five girls" on the road as The Marvelettes, a proposition the actual members rejected. The label later replaced a pregnant Wonder Young on tour with Florence Ballard from The Supremes, ensuring that touring contracts for the group specified "five Marvelettes." "Not only that, but at one point when Wonder had been pregnant, Motown had replaced him on the road with Florence Ballard from the Supremes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Name Change to The Marvelettes
podcast.body: The group's name, The Cassin Yet, was deemed unsuitable, and Barry Gordy supposedly renamed them The Marvelettes after hearing them sing and exclaiming, "those girls are marvels." This new name marked their official birth as a Motown act. "The name they were eventually given supposedly came after Barry Gordy heard them sing it and said, those girls are marvels."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Origin as The Delvid Matt
podcast.body: Gladys Horton, at just 14 years old, formed an earlier group named The Delvid Matt in Inkster, Michigan. This group released one single before disbanding, but Gladys remained determined to pursue music. "When Horton was only 14, she had formed a group called The Delvid Matt, who made one single, and the Delvid Matt had split up."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Outperforming The Supremes
podcast.body: The Marvelettes consistently achieved greater chart success than The Supremes for a two-year period, securing hits while The Supremes struggled to break into the Top 100. "the Supremes now being passed in chart success, not only by the Marvelettes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Rejection of "Where Did Our Love Go"
podcast.body: The Marvelettes, including member Catherine Anderson, were offered the backing track for "Where Did Our Love Go" by Holland-Dozier-Holland for a potential album, but they chose to reject the "dreadful song," opting for other material instead. They subsequently advised The Supremes to avoid it if possible. "The Marvelettes were played a couple of backing tracks, which have been proposed as their next recording, and they chose to dump the 8 bar one."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Rejection of "Where Did Our Love Go"
podcast.body: The Marvelettes missed the opportunity for a major hit when Gladys Horton disliked the song "Where Did Our Love Go," which was written for them by Holland, Dozier, and Holland. She found the song "too simplistic," leading Motown to offer it instead to The Supremes, who were then known internally as "the no-hit Supremes." "Holland, Doge and Holland had written a song for them, but Gladys didn't like it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Shift to Wonder Young as Sole Lead Vocalist
podcast.body: After a period of less successful follow-ups, Smokey Robinson took over the group's production and decided to make Wonder Young the primary lead vocalist, replacing Gladys Horton, who had sung lead on their earlier hits. This change coincided with a second commercial wind for the group as a trio. "Smokey Robinson took over their production and decided to start using Wander as the lead vocalist, rather than Gladys, who had sung lead on their hits up to that point."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Unannounced Group Split
podcast.body: The Marvelettes informally dissolved without any official announcement; they simply stopped receiving bookings for tours and went their separate ways. Motown, owning the group name, subsequently sold it off, allowing other groups to tour under The Marvelettes' name without any original members. "The groups split up though nothing was announced, they just didn't get booked and anymore tours, and went their separate ways."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Wanda Young's Personal Tragedies and Mental Health Decline
podcast.body: Wonder Young experienced a series of personal crises, including cocaine and alcohol abuse, the shooting death of her younger sister, and having her drink spiked during a European tour. These events severely impacted her mental health, leading to lasting problems for over 50 years and rendering her unable to perform regularly for decades. "She was never the same again, and has had mental health problems for the last 50 years."
